claim: Neuromasts of the posterior lateral line in medaka are composed of two independent life-long lineages with different embryonic origins.
source: Here we show that neuromasts of the posterior lateral line in medaka are composed of two independent life-long lineages with different embryonic origins.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by clonal analysis and 4D imaging data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The neural lineage induces the formation of an outer, border cell lineage (nBC) from the skin epithelium.
source: Clonal analysis and 4D imaging revealed a hierarchical organisation with instructing and responding roles: an inner, neural lineage induces the formation of an outer, border cell lineage (nBC) from the skin epithelium.
evidence: This claim is supported by 4D imaging data showing the conversion of epithelial cells to nBCs and experimental ablation studies.

claim: The neural lineage is necessary and sufficient to generate nBCs.
source: Our results demonstrate that the neural lineage is necessary and sufficient to generate nBCs highlighting self-organisation principles at the level of the entire embryo.
evidence: This is supported by ablation experiments showing that ectopic neural lineage induces nBCs and absence of neural lineage prevents nBC formation.

claim: Tg(Eya1:EGFP) is expressed in all cells of the migrating primordium and during organogenesis.
source: The transgenic line (Tg) Tg(Eya1:EGFP) (Seleit et al., 2017) is expressed in all cells of the migrating primordium and during organogenesis, but is restricted to hair cells and internal support cells located underneath HCs in mature organs (Figure 1A,A').
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A,A' and cited from a previous publication.

claim: Tg(Eya1:EGFP) is restricted to hair cells and internal support cells in mature organs.
source: The transgenic line (Tg) Tg(Eya1:EGFP) (Seleit et al., 2017) is expressed in all cells of the migrating primordium and during organogenesis, but is restricted to hair cells and internal support cells located underneath HCs in mature organs (Figure 1A,A').
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1A,A' showing expression pattern in mature neuromasts.

claim: The enhancer trap neuromK8:H2B-EGFP labels all support cells and mantle cells.
source: The newly generated enhancer trap neuromK8:H2B-EGFP stably labels all support cells and mantle cells (Figure 1B,B')(See Materials and methods).
evidence: This is shown by imaging data in Figure 1B,B' demonstrating the expression pattern of this transgenic line.

claim: Tg(K15:H2B-RFP) labels a subset of neuromK8 positive cells that form a peripheral ring in mature neuromasts.
source: Additionally, the Tg(K15:H2B-RFP) labels a subset of the neuromK8 positive cells that form a peripheral ring in mature neuromasts (Figure 1C–C') and are Sox2 positive (Figure 1D–D'').
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figures 1C-C' and 1D-D'' showing the expression pattern and Sox2 co-localization.

claim: K15 positive cells form a peripheral ring in mature neuromasts and are Sox2 positive.
source: Additionally, the Tg(K15:H2B-RFP) labels a subset of the neuromK8 positive cells that form a peripheral ring in mature neuromasts (Figure 1C–C') and are Sox2 positive (Figure 1D–D'').
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining data in Figure 1D-D'' demonstrating Sox2 expression in K15+ cells.

claim: EYFP positive cells wrap the hair cells of the organ.
source: A 3D reconstruction of triple transgenic Tg(K15:mEYFP), Tg(K15:H2B-RFP), Tg(Eya1:EGFP) neuromasts indicates that EYFP positive cells are wrapping the hair cells of the organ (Figure 1E and Video 1), a distinctive morphology and position that characterises mantle cells (Jones and Corwin, 1993; Steiner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3D reconstruction data shown in Figure 1E and Video 1, and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The morphology and position of EYFP positive cells characterizes them as mantle cells.
source: A 3D reconstruction of triple transgenic Tg(K15:mEYFP), Tg(K15:H2B-RFP), Tg(Eya1:EGFP) neuromasts indicates that EYFP positive cells are wrapping the hair cells of the organ (Figure 1E and Video 1), a distinctive morphology and position that characterises mantle cells (Jones and Corwin, 1993; Steiner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the 3D reconstruction data and supported by citations to previous characterizations of mantle cells.

claim: Both neuromK8:H2B-EGFP and Tg(K15:H2B-RFP) label skin epithelia on the entire body of juvenile and adult medaka fish.
source: Both neuromK8:H2B-EGFP and Tg(K15:H2B-RFP) also label skin epithelia on the entire body of juvenile and adult medaka fish.
evidence: This is observed in the imaging data presented in Figures 1B and 1C showing expression throughout the body surface.

claim: K15+ mantle cells are consistently surrounded by an outer ring of cells that feature elongated nuclei.
source: While observing neuromasts counterstained with DAPI, we noticed that K15 positive (K15+) mantle cells are consistently surrounded by an outer ring of cells that feature elongated nuclei (Figure 2A,A').
evidence: This is demonstrated by DAPI staining data shown in Figure 2A,A' across multiple neuromasts.

claim: Elongated nuclei surrounding mantle cells are present in all neuromasts in medaka, including ventral, midline and dorsal neuromasts on the posterior lateral line, and neuromasts of the anterior lateral lines in both juveniles and adults.
source: This is the case for all neuromasts in medaka, including ventral, midline and dorsal neuromasts on the posterior lateral line, and neuromasts of the anterior lateral lines in both juveniles and adults (N > 100 neuromasts).
evidence: This is based on observations across more than 100 neuromasts in different locations and developmental stages.

claim: The membranes of border cells are intimately associated with those of mantle cells, often producing cytoplasmic protrusions into one another.
source: Electron microscopy revealed that the membranes of border cells are intimately associated with those of mantle cells, often producing cytoplasmic protrusions into one another (Figure 2B–B''')
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2B-B'''.

claim: Desmosomes exist between mantle cells and nBCs.
source: In addition we also observed desmosomes between MCs and nBCs (Figure 2C–C'').
evidence: This is shown by electron microscopy data in Figure 2C-C'' identifying desmosome structures.

claim: A proportion of nBCs are EGFP positive in Tg(K15:H2B-EGFP) medaka larvae.
source: Using iterative imaging on Tg(K15:H2B-EGFP) medaka larvae, we detected that a proportion of nBCs are EGFP positive (Figure 2D) but this expression decays within the following days.
evidence: This is demonstrated by iterative imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: EGFP expression in nBCs decays within days after initial detection.
source: Using iterative imaging on Tg(K15:H2B-EGFP) medaka larvae, we detected that a proportion of nBCs are EGFP positive (Figure 2D) but this expression decays within the following days.
evidence: This is observed through iterative imaging showing loss of EGFP signal over time.

claim: The transient nature of EGFP expression in nBCs suggests they could originate from K15+ cells and inherit the fluorescent protein.
source: The transient nature of this expression suggests nBCs could originate from K15+ cells and inherit the fluorescent protein, which in this case would be acting as a short-term lineage tracer.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of transient EGFP expression in nBCs.

claim: Mantle cells expand and generate support and hair cells.
source: The lineage analysis of 152 clones in 111 neuromasts (21 embryos) from 9 and up to 21 days suggested two independent short-term lineages. One lineage involves mantle cells that expand and generate support and hair cells (Figure 3C–D'') - the neural lineage - while the other lineage was restricted to neuromast border cells (Figure 3E–E'').
evidence: This is demonstrated by clonal lineage tracing data shown in Figures 3C-D'' tracking mantle cell progeny over time.

claim: Border cells constitute a lineage that is restricted to neuromast border cells.
source: The lineage analysis of 152 clones in 111 neuromasts (21 embryos) from 9 and up to 21 days suggested two independent short-term lineages. One lineage involves mantle cells that expand and generate support and hair cells (Figure 3C–D'') - the neural lineage - while the other lineage was restricted to neuromast border cells (Figure 3E–E'').
evidence: This is demonstrated by clonal lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3E-E'' showing nBC-restricted clones.

claim: 72 neuromasts contained clones that were restricted to the neural lineage throughout the timeline of the experiment.
source: We observed that 72 neuromasts contained clones that were restricted to the neural lineage throughout the timeline of the experiment.
evidence: This is based on quantification of clonal analysis data from 152 clones in 111 neuromasts.

claim: Neural lineage clones never generated a labelled nBC.
source: Intriguingly, they never generated a labelled nBC, suggesting that border cells do not originate from this lineage.
evidence: This is observed across 72 neuromasts with neural lineage clones that never included nBCs.

claim: 21 neuromasts contained labelled nBCs, which did not contribute to the neural lineage.
source: We also observed 21 neuromasts containing labelled nBCs, which did not contribute to the neural lineage (Figure 3E–E').
evidence: This is based on clonal analysis data showing nBC-restricted clones in 21 neuromasts.

claim: The caudal neuromast cluster (CNC) contains an increasing amount of neuromasts as fish age.
source: The CNC contains an increasing amount of neuromasts as fish age - the older the fish, the more neuromasts in the CNC.
evidence: This is observed through imaging of fish at different ages showing progressive increase in neuromast numbers.

claim: NeuromastP0 is the last neuromast formed by the migrating primordium.
source: Neuromasts in the CNC are generated post-embryonically, presumably from a founder, embryonic neuromast - neuromastP0 (Figure 4A,B). NeuromastP0 is the last neuromast formed by the migrating primordium as it comes to a halt and takes its position in a highly stereotypic way on what will become part of the caudal fin.
evidence: This is based on observations of primordium migration and neuromast deposition patterns shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: NeuromastP0 is the source of all new organs in the CNC.
source: We confirmed that it is the source of all new organs in the CNC by two photon laser ablations, which revealed that eliminating the neuromastP0 at eight days post-fertilisation (dpf)(Figure 4C,C') results in an adult missing the CNC on the experimental side but with a wild-type CNC on the contralateral, control side (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ablation experiments shown in Figures 4C-E where removal of neuromastP0 prevents CNC formation.

claim: Eliminating neuromastP0 at 8 dpf results in an adult missing the CNC on the experimental side.
source: We confirmed that it is the source of all new organs in the CNC by two photon laser ablations, which revealed that eliminating the neuromastP0 at eight days post-fertilisation (dpf)(Figure 4C,C') results in an adult missing the CNC on the experimental side but with a wild-type CNC on the contralateral, control side (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is shown by ablation experiments in Figure 4 comparing ablated and control sides in adults.

claim: Both neural and nBC lineages are maintained by dedicated, fate-restricted stem cells.
source: The analysis of long-term clones in the CNC revealed that both neural and nBC lineages are maintained by dedicated, fate-restricted stem cells (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by long-term clonal analysis data shown in Figures 5B-D tracking lineages for up to 18 months.

claim: 92% of neuromasts contain fate restricted clones, comprising either the neural lineage (34.8%) or the nBC lineage (57.1%).
source: We observed that 92% of neuromasts contain fate restricted clones, comprising either the neural lineage (34.8%, N = 39/112 neuromasts)(Figure 5B,D) or the nBC lineage (57.1%, N = 64/112 neuromasts)(Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is based on quantification of long-term clonal analysis data from 112 labeled neuromasts in 47 CNCs.

claim: 8% of neuromasts show co-occurrence of labelled cells in both lineages.
source: The remaining 8% of neuromasts show co-occurrence of labelled cells in both lineages (N = 9/112 neuromasts)(Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on quantification of long-term clonal analysis showing 9 out of 112 neuromasts with both lineages labeled.

claim: The ratio of co-labelled clones drops to 5.1% when restricting analysis to CNCs with ≤50% of neuromasts labelled per cluster.
source: By restricting the analysis to CNCs with sparse labelling (≤50% of neuromasts labelled per cluster), the ratio of co-labelled clones drops further (5.1%, 4/79 labelled neuromasts in 39 CNCs), and disappears when we select for an even lower recombination efficiency (≤25% of neuromasts labelled per cluster, 0/17 labelled neuromasts in 15 CNCs).
evidence: This is based on quantification of clonal data with different labeling efficiency thresholds.

claim: Co-labeling disappears when selecting for ≤25% of neuromasts labelled per cluster.
source: By restricting the analysis to CNCs with sparse labelling (≤50% of neuromasts labelled per cluster), the ratio of co-labelled clones drops further (5.1%, 4/79 labelled neuromasts in 39 CNCs), and disappears when we select for an even lower recombination efficiency (≤25% of neuromasts labelled per cluster, 0/17 labelled neuromasts in 15 CNCs).
evidence: This is based on quantification showing 0 out of 17 neuromasts with co-labeling at low recombination efficiency.

claim: As few as four K15+ cells were sufficient to regenerate the entire neural lineage of a neuromast.
source: Notably, as few as four K15+ cells were sufficient to regenerate the entire neural lineage of a neuromast.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ablation and regeneration experiments where 4 surviving K15+ cells regenerated complete neuromasts.

claim: Mantle cells have the potential of reconstituting all the cell types within the neural lineage of an organ after severe injury.
source: These results indicate that mantle cells have the potential of reconstituting all the cell types within the neural lineage of an organ after severe injury.
evidence: This is inferred from regeneration experiments showing complete neural lineage reconstitution from surviving mantle cells.

claim: Mantle cell derived clones contained mantle and support cells in 30 neuromasts in 12 fish.
source: Our analysis revealed that mantle cell derived clones contained mantle and support cells (N = 30 neuromasts in 12 fish) (Figure 7D')
evidence: This is based on clonal analysis using K15:CreERT2 driver showing mantle cell progeny in 30 neuromasts.

claim: Mantle cell derived clones contained all cell types of the neural lineage in 8 neuromasts in 5 fish.
source: and in some cases all cell types of the neural lineage (Figure 7E') (N = 8 neuromasts in five fish).
evidence: This is based on clonal analysis using K15:CreERT2 driver showing complete neural lineage in 8 neuromasts.

claim: K15+ mantle cells function as neuromast neural stem cells during homeostatic growth, post-embryonic formation of new neuromasts and organ regeneration.
source: Altogether, our results indicate that K15+ mantle cells function as neuromast neural stem cells during homeostatic growth, post-embryonic formation of new neuromasts and organ regeneration.
evidence: This is concluded from multiple lines of evidence including clonal analysis, regeneration experiments, and long-term lineage tracing.

claim: Clones containing border cells reproducibly continue into skin epithelial cells in the vicinity of the neuromasts in 100% of injected embryos (N = 40 neuromasts).
source: Notably, we observed that clones containing border cells reproducibly continue into skin epithelial cells in the vicinity of the neuromasts both in injected embryos (100%, N = 40 neuromasts)(Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,D) as well as in the previously described long term lineage analysis (100%, N > 100 neuromasts)(Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is observed in mosaic clonal analysis showing continuity between nBCs and epithelial cells in all cases examined.

claim: Clones containing border cells continue into skin epithelial cells in 100% of cases in long term lineage analysis (N > 100 neuromasts).
source: Notably, we observed that clones containing border cells reproducibly continue into skin epithelial cells in the vicinity of the neuromasts both in injected embryos (100%, N = 40 neuromasts)(Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,D) as well as in the previously described long term lineage analysis (100%, N > 100 neuromasts)(Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is observed in long-term clonal analysis showing continuity between nBCs and epithelial cells in all cases.

claim: Three to four K15+ epithelial cells respond to the arrival of the neural stem cell precursors.
source: As the developing midline neuromasts reach the horizontal myoseptum they come into contact with the overlying epithelial cells. Promptly, three to four K15+ epithelial cells (red, green and blue dots in Figure 8A) respond to the arrival of the neural stem cell precursors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by 4D time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 8A and Videos 2-4.

claim: Epithelial cells undergo significant morphological changes resulting in the characteristic elongated shape of border cell nuclei over a period of 72 hours.
source: Over a period of 72 hours, these epithelial cells undergo significant morphological changes resulting in the characteristic elongated shape of border cell nuclei.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging tracking epithelial cell transformation over 72 hours.

claim: Both ventral and midline neuromasts of the posterior lateral line system in medaka, as well as neuromasts of the anterior lateral line, trigger the same behaviour in the surrounding epithelium.
source: Both ventral and midline neuromasts of the posterior lateral line system in medaka, as well as neuromasts of the anterior lateral line (aLL), trigger the same behaviour in the surrounding epithelium (five ventral neuromasts and four midline neuromasts in the pLL and two neuromasts in the aLL, N = 5 embryos).
evidence: This is observed across multiple neuromast types through 4D imaging in 5 embryos.

claim: The arrival of neural stem cell precursors is accompanied by a change in nuclear morphology of skin epithelial cells that were present at the place of arrival.
source: These movies indicate that the arrival of neural stem cell precursors is accompanied by a change in nuclear morphology of skin epithelial cells that were present at the place of arrival.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging showing temporal correlation between neural precursor arrival and epithelial cell transformation.

claim: A change in cellular morphology coincides with a change in nuclear shape during nBC induction.
source: The results revealed that a change in cellular morphology coincides with a change in nuclear shape (Figure 8B,B', white and green asterisks, Video 5 and quantifications in Figure 8—figure supplement 1), as observed in clones that contain both skin epithelial cells and nBCs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of double-labeled clones showing both nuclear and cellular shape changes, with quantification in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: nBCs are continuous with the suprabasal layer of the skin epithelium rather than with more superficial epithelial cells.
source: A detailed analysis of nBC clones revealed that these are continuous with the suprabasal layer of the skin epithelium rather than with more superficial epithelial cells (see Figure 8—figure supplement 2 and Video 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by z-stack imaging analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2 and Video 5.

claim: K15+ cells of the neural lineage extended numerous cytoplasmic processes during the early phase of organ formation.
source: We observed that K15+ cells of the neural lineage extended numerous cytoplasmic processes during the early phase of organ formation (Figure 8—figure supplement 3) (N = 8 clones in five larvae).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of K15:mYFP labeled clones showing cytoplasmic protrusions in 8 clones.

claim: Cytoplasmic processes from neural lineage cells were dynamic and transient.
source: Iterative imaging of K15+ clones revealed that these processes were dynamic and transient (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C–C''), and eventually disappeared by the time of organ maturation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by iterative imaging showing appearance and disappearance of cytoplasmic processes over time.

claim: Cytoplasmic processes from neural lineage cells disappeared by the time of organ maturation.
source: Iterative imaging of K15+ clones revealed that these processes were dynamic and transient (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C–C''), and eventually disappeared by the time of organ maturation.
evidence: This is shown by time-series imaging tracking cytoplasmic processes from early organogenesis to maturation.

claim: nBCs are recruited from K15+ suprabasal skin epithelial cells.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that nBCs are recruited from K15+ suprabasal skin epithelial cells and reveal numerous cytoplasmic processes from the neural lineage during the induction phase.
evidence: This is concluded from multiple lines of evidence including 4D imaging, clonal analysis, and morphological characterization.

claim: Neuromasts from Poecilia formosa displayed nuclei that are highly reminiscent of nBCs and that were adjacent to cells with the nuclear morphology of mantle cells.
source: Neuromasts from both fish displayed nuclei that are highly reminiscent of nBCs and that were adjacent to cells with the nuclear morphology of mantle cells (Figure 9A–D) (N = 10 neuromasts in a single 1 month old Poecilia formosa fish, N = 5 neuromasts in three zebrafish larvae).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DAPI staining of Poecilia formosa neuromasts shown in Figure 9A-B.

claim: Neuromasts from zebrafish displayed nuclei that are highly reminiscent of nBCs and that were adjacent to cells with the nuclear morphology of mantle cells.
source: Neuromasts from both fish displayed nuclei that are highly reminiscent of nBCs and that were adjacent to cells with the nuclear morphology of mantle cells (Figure 9A–D) (N = 10 neuromasts in a single 1 month old Poecilia formosa fish, N = 5 neuromasts in three zebrafish larvae).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DAPI staining of zebrafish neuromasts shown in Figure 9C-D.

claim: Tg(o.l.K15:H2B-EGFP) shows expression in the skin epithelium and neuromast mantle cells of 5 days post fertilization zebrafish larvae.
source: To better characterise nBCs in zebrafish, we generated a Tg(o.l.K15:H2B-EGFP) using the medaka K15 promoter sequence and observed expression in the skin epithelium and neuromast mantle cells of 5 days post fertilization larvae (Figure 9E) (N = 5 neuromasts in three larvae).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of the transgenic zebrafish line shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Zebrafish nBCs transiently expressed low levels of H2B-EGFP.
source: Furthermore, and as shown for medaka (Figure 2D), zebrafish nBCs transiently expressed low levels of H2B-EGFP suggesting they could also originate from skin epithelial cells (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of Tg(o.l.K15:H2B-EGFP) zebrafish showing EGFP in nBCs as shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Zebrafish nBCs are induced from the skin epithelium soon after the deposition of the neural lineage by the migrating primordium.
source: These movies show that despite the different way in which neuromasts are formed in both fish models (Seleit et al., 2017), zebrafish nBCs are also induced from the skin epithelium soon after the deposition of the neural lineage by the migrating primordium (N = 4 neuromasts in two embryos).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging in double transgenic zebrafish shown in Video 6.

claim: Both the existence and induction of nBCs are conserved in distantly related teleost fish.
source: Overall, these results indicate that both the existence and induction of nBCs are conserved in distantly related teleost fish.
evidence: This is concluded from observations of nBCs in medaka, Poecilia formosa, and zebrafish.

claim: The ablation of single nBCs results in an immediate reaction of the directly adjacent mantle stem cells.
source: The ablation of single nBCs in Tg(K15:H2B-EGFP) results in an immediate reaction of the directly adjacent mantle stem cells (Figure 10A–A' and Video 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ablation experiments shown in Figure 10A-A' and Video 7.

claim: Ablation of single nBCs leads to a retraction of mantle cells towards the centre of the neuromast leading to a notch-shaped organ with a distorted architecture.
source: This involves a retraction of mantle cells towards the centre of the neuromast leading to a notch-shaped organ with a distorted architecture (N = 10 neuromast distributed in seven medaka embryos) (Figure 10A'', A''' Video 7), suggesting they were detached from their physical anchor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging after nBC ablation showing organ shape changes in 10 neuromasts.

claim: The neural lineage is maintained and the integrity of the organ is re-established when new border cells re-appear within a week after nBC removal.
source: We observed that the neural lineage is maintained and the integrity of the organ is re-established when new border cells re-appear (Figure 10B''), a process that happens within a week after nBC removal (N = 8 neuromasts in four embryos).
evidence: This is demonstrated by iterative imaging after nBC ablation showing organ recovery in Figure 10B''.

claim: nBCs are crucial for maintaining neuromast integrity and architecture.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that nBCs are crucial for maintaining neuromast integrity and architecture and suggest they act as a physical niche for K15+ neural stem cells.
evidence: This is concluded from ablation experiments showing disruption of organ architecture upon nBC removal.

claim: nBCs act as a physical niche for K15+ neural stem cells.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that nBCs are crucial for maintaining neuromast integrity and architecture and suggest they act as a physical niche for K15+ neural stem cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the intimate association between nBCs and mantle cells, and the effects of nBC ablation on organ architecture.

claim: Irrespective of how many neural clusters are generated by the primordium, and regardless of the final position along the anterior-posterior axis, all mature neuromasts contain nBCs.
source: Our previous observations suggest a leading role for the neural lineage, since left and right pLLs in medaka larvae often have an unequal number of neuromasts located in undetermined positions (Seleit et al., 2017). Irrespective of how many neural clusters are generated by the primordium, and regardless of the final position along the anterior-posterior axis, all mature neuromasts contain nBCs.
evidence: This is observed across all neuromasts examined regardless of their number or position.

claim: Injection of Cas9 mRNA and two gRNAs directed against medaka neurogenin-1 resulted in juveniles with an increased amount of pLL neuromasts.
source: The injection of Cas9 mRNA and two gRNAs directed against medaka neurogenin-1 into Tg(Eya1:EGFP) or Tg(Eya1:H2B-EGFP) resulted in juveniles with an increased amount of pLL neuromasts (Figure 11A and Figure 11—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CRISPR/Cas9 experiments shown in Figure 11A and Figure 11—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ectopic midline neuromasts are composed of neural lineage and nBCs.
source: Our results show that ectopic midline neuromasts are composed of neural lineage and nBCs (Figure 11C–I) (N = 33 neuromasts in two larvae).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DAPI staining of ectopic neuromasts shown in Figure 11B-H.

claim: The presence of the neural lineage is sufficient to drive ectopic induction of epithelial cells into border cells.
source: This suggests that the presence of the neural lineage is sufficient to drive ectopic induction of epithelial cells into border cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ectopic neural lineage cells induce nBCs in ngn1 mutants.

claim: Ablation of the primordium before deposition of the last neuromast results in fish lacking the CNC.
source: Complementarily, ablation of the primordium before deposition of the last neuromast results in fish lacking the CNC (Figure 11J,K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ablation experiments shown in Figure 11J,K.

claim: The absence of induced border cells on the ablated side was confirmed, as opposed to their presence on the non-ablated, control side.
source: A detailed analysis of DAPI stained caudal fins revealed the absence of induced border cells on the ablated side, as opposed to their presence on the non-ablated, control side (Figure 11J',K') (N = 4 CNCs of 4 fish).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DAPI staining comparing ablated and control sides shown in Figure 11J',K'.

claim: The neural lineage is both necessary and sufficient to induce the conversion of epithelial cells into neuromast border cells in situ.
source: Altogether, our results demonstrate that the neural lineage is both necessary and sufficient to induce the conversion of epithelial cells into neuromast border cells in situ.
evidence: This is concluded from both gain-of-function (ectopic neuromasts) and loss-of-function (ablation) experiments.

claim: Mantle cells constitute bona fide neuromast neural stem cells during homeostasis, growth and organ regeneration.
source: We prove that mantle cells constitute bona fide neuromast neural stem cells during homeostasis, growth and organ regeneration.
evidence: This is concluded from multiple lines of evidence including long-term lineage tracing, regeneration experiments, and clonal analysis.

claim: nBCs constitute a different lineage that never crosses boundaries with the neural lineage maintained by mantle cells in medaka.
source: We demonstrate that in medaka, nBCs constitute a different lineage that never crosses boundaries with the neural lineage maintained by mantle cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by long-term lineage tracing showing fate-restricted clones in both lineages.

claim: Border cells do not originate from the pLL primordium but rather from the suprabasal skin epithelium.
source: We track border cells back to earlier developmental stages both in medaka and zebrafish, and reveal that they do not originate from the pLL primordium but rather from the suprabasal skin epithelium, defining neuromasts as composite organs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by 4D imaging and clonal analysis showing nBC origin from epithelium.

claim: Neural stem cells are necessary and sufficient to induce the conversion of epithelial cells into nBCs.
source: Finally, we show that neural stem cells are necessary and sufficient to induce the conversion of epithelial cells into nBCs, and that the ablation of nBCs disrupts the architecture of the organ.
evidence: This is demonstrated by gain-of-function and loss-of-function experiments showing induction and necessity of neural lineage.

claim: The ablation of nBCs disrupts the architecture of the organ.
source: Finally, we show that neural stem cells are necessary and sufficient to induce the conversion of epithelial cells into nBCs, and that the ablation of nBCs disrupts the architecture of the organ.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ablation experiments showing organ distortion after nBC removal.

claim: Hair cells are continuously lost and replaced under homeostatic conditions throughout the life of fish.
source: Since HCs are continuously lost and replaced under homeostatic conditions (Cruz et al., 2015; Williams and Holder, 2000) and in response to injury (Hernández et al., 2007; López-Schier and Hudspeth, 2006) throughout the life of fish (Pinto-Teixeira et al., 2015), the existence of stem cells capable of constantly replenishing HCs has been proposed.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on hair cell turnover.

claim: Hair cells are replaced in response to injury throughout the life of fish.
source: Since HCs are continuously lost and replaced under homeostatic conditions (Cruz et al., 2015; Williams and Holder, 2000) and in response to injury (Hernández et al., 2007; López-Schier and Hudspeth, 2006) throughout the life of fish (Pinto-Teixeira et al., 2015), the existence of stem cells capable of constantly replenishing HCs has been proposed.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on hair cell regeneration.

claim: New neuromasts are continuously added to the lateral line system during the lifetime of fish, presumably to cope with an increasing body size.
source: The presence of neuromast stem cells has also been inferred from the fact that new neuromasts are continuously added to the lateral line system during the lifetime of fish, presumably to cope with an increasing body size (Dufourcq et al., 2006; Ghysen and Dambly-Chaudière, 2007; Wada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on post-embryonic neuromast formation.

claim: The peripheral ring of mantle cells plays a major role in new organ formation.
source: It has been reported that the peripheral ring of mantle cells plays a major role in new organ formation (Dufourcq et al., 2006; Jones and Corwin, 1993; Stone, 1933; Wada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on mantle cell function.

claim: A linear model has been proposed in which mantle cells give rise to support cells that in turn replenish lost hair cells.
source: This has led to the proposition of a linear model in which mantle cells give rise to support cells that in turn replenish lost hair cells (Ghysen and Dambly-Chaudière, 2007).
evidence: This is a model proposed in previous literature cited here.

claim: The transition from support to hair cells is strongly supported by a large body of experimental evidence.
source: The transition from support to hair cells has been heavily investigated in the past decade and is strongly supported by a large body of experimental evidence (Hernández et al., 2007; López-Schier and Hudspeth, 2006; Ma et al., 2008; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015; Wibowo et al., 2011; Williams and Holder, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies on support to hair cell transition.

claim: The proposed transition of mantle into support cells has not yet been shown.
source: However, the proposed transition of mantle into support cells has not yet been shown and it is still unknown where the stem cells of the neuromasts reside (Pinto-Teixeira et al., 2015).
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge based on previous literature.

claim: Upon repeated injury of the hair cell population coupled with a depletion of support cells, mantle cells re-enter the cell cycle.
source: An interesting observation is that upon repeated injury of the hair cell population coupled with a depletion of support cells, mantle cells re-enter the cell cycle (Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015), but their precise role during homeostasis and regeneration remains unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on mantle cell proliferation.

claim: The current view posits support cells as multipotent progenitors capable of self-renewing and differentiation.
source: The current view posits support cells as multipotent progenitors capable of self-renewing and differentiation and suggests a niche role for mantle cells influencing SC proliferative behaviour and fate (Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the prevailing model in the field based on cited literature.

claim: Medaka and zebrafish diverged approximately 250 million years ago.
source: the evolutionarily distant zebrafish, Danio rerio – which diverged from medaka ca. 250 millon years ago (Schartl et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an established fact from evolutionary biology cited from previous literature.

claim: The loss-of-function of neurogenin-1 or erbb results in the formation of ectopic neuromasts in zebrafish by neural lineage interneuromast cells that re-enter the cell cycle.
source: The loss-of-function of neurogenin-1 or erbb has been shown to result in the formation of ectopic neuromasts in zebrafish by neural lineage interneuromast cells that re-enter the cell cycle (Grant et al., 2005; López-Schier and Hudspeth, 2005; Lush and Piotrowski, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on neurogenin-1 and erbb function.

claim: The dynamics of neuromast regeneration resembles the formation of secondary neuromasts during embryonic development.
source: Interestingly, the dynamics of neuromast regeneration seems to resemble the formation of secondary neuromasts during embryonic development (Seleit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of regeneration dynamics with developmental observations cited from previous work.

claim: The efficient regeneration of neuromasts in medaka contrasts with its reported inability to adequately regenerate its heart upon mechanical injury.
source: Intriguingly, the efficient regeneration of neuromasts in medaka contrasts with its reported inability to adequately regenerate its heart upon mechanical injury (Ito et al., 2014).
evidence: This comparison is made based on citation to a previous study on medaka heart regeneration.

claim: Regeneration enhancer elements exist in zebrafish and can drive tissue specific regenerative responses to injury.
source: It has recently been shown that regeneration enhancer elements exist in zebrafish and can drive tissue specific regenerative responses to injury (Kang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study on regeneration enhancer elements.

claim: Numerous short-term studies in zebrafish have reported that both during homeostasis and regeneration HCs are produced by post-mitotic hair cell precursors.
source: Numerous short-term studies in zebrafish, however, have reported that both during homeostasis and regeneration HCs are produced by post-mitotic hair cell precursors (Hernández et al., 2007; Kniss et al., 2016) and proliferation of support cells (Hernández et al., 2007; López-Schier and Hudspeth, 2006; Pinto-Teixeira et al., 2015; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
evidence: This summarizes findings from multiple cited studies on hair cell production.

claim: Several studies have reported the existence of compartments or territories within the neuromasts that permit either self-renewal of support cells or differentiation into HCs.
source: In the past years, several studies have reported the existence of compartments or territories within the neuromasts that permit either self-renewal of support cells or differentiation into HCs (Pinto-Teixeira et al., 2015; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015; Wibowo et al., 2011).
evidence: This summarizes findings from multiple cited studies on neuromast organization.

claim: The formation of the lens in the vertebrate retina was the first reported case of tissue induction.
source: The formation of the lens in the vertebrate retina was the first reported case of tissue induction. There, the developing optic vesicle (composed of neural progenitors) contacts the surface ectoderm to induce a lens placode from previous ectoderm cells (Cvekl and Ashery-Padan, 2014; Gunhaga, 2011), (Bailey et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an established fact from developmental biology supported by citations.

claim: The developing optic vesicle contacts the surface ectoderm to induce a lens placode from ectoderm cells.
source: The formation of the lens in the vertebrate retina was the first reported case of tissue induction. There, the developing optic vesicle (composed of neural progenitors) contacts the surface ectoderm to induce a lens placode from previous ectoderm cells (Cvekl and Ashery-Padan, 2014; Gunhaga, 2011), (Bailey et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on lens induction.

claim: Neuromast neural lineage cells are Eya1+ as retinal progenitors.
source: Neuromast neural lineage cells are Eya1+ as retinal progenitors, and they induce a cell fate change in K15+ ectodermal cells.
evidence: This is based on the expression patterns observed in the transgenic lines used in this study.

claim: The stem cell niche is key for stem cell maintenance in plants, invertebrates and vertebrates.
source: The stem cell niche is key for stem cell maintenance in plants, invertebrates and vertebrates..
evidence: This is established knowledge in stem cell biology.

claim: The concept of the stem cell niche was introduced by Schofield during the late 70's.
source: The concept of the stem cell niche was introduced by Schofield during the late 70's (Schofield, 1978), and since then is defined as the stem cell microenvironment and architecture (Fuchs et al., 2004; Morrison and Spradling, 2008; Nystul and Spradling, 2006; Scadden, 2014).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to the original work and subsequent reviews.

claim: In the fly testis, germ stem cells are in contact with Hub cells (niche cells), and this interaction defines stemness through a series of well defined signalling pathways.
source: In the fly testis, germ stem cells are in contact with Hub cells (niche cells), and this interaction defines stemness through a series of well defined signalling pathways (Tulina and Matunis, 2001; Xie and Spradling, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Drosophila stem cell niche.

claim: Many cell types in the bone marrow have been reported as hematopoetic stem cell (HSC) regulators and contributors to the hematopoietic niche, including endothelial cells, LepR+, adipocytes, Schwann cells, nerve fibers and even macrophages and megakaryocytes.
source: In contrast, many cell types in the bone marrow have been reported as hematopoetic stem cell (HSC) regulators and contributors to the hematopoietic niche, including endothelial cells, LepR+, adipocytes, Schwann cells, nerve fibers and even macrophages and megakaryocytes (Bruns et al., 2014; Christopher et al., 2011; Méndez-Ferrer et al., 2008; Scadden, 2014; Yamazaki et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on the hematopoietic niche.

claim: Mouse embryonic stem cells will self-renew upon culture conditions, generate any differentiated cell type if transplanted into a blastula but produce teratomas if implanted in an adult.
source: Many examples have been reported on how stem cells can act upon changes in their microenvironment. Mouse embryonic stem cells will self-renew upon culture conditions, generate any differentiated cell type if transplanted into a blastula but produce teratomas if implanted in an adult (reviewed in (Fuchs et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about embryonic stem cells cited from a review.

claim: Luminal stem cells in the mammary gland are bipotent in an embryonic niche, unipotent in the adult niche, and bipotent again upon loss of their basal counterpart.
source: Luminal stem cells in the mammary gland are bipotent in an embryonic niche, unipotent in the adult niche, and bipotent again upon loss of their basal counterpart (Van Keymeulen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on mammary gland stem cells.

claim: Neoblasts in planarians generate the cell types of their surroundings, but upon excision of a major part of the body they can produce distal cell types and even generate an entire new organism.
source: Neoblasts in planarians generate the cell types of their surroundings, but upon excision of a major part of the body they can produce distal cell types and even generate an entire new organism (Gurley et al., 2008; Sánchez Alvarado, 2003; Wagner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on planarian regeneration.

claim: Most niche cells have a different lineage than their respective stem cells.
source: Most niche cells have a different lineage than their respective stem cells (Fuchs et al., 2004), which raises fundamental developmental questions such as how do these cell types come together (Tamplin et al., 2015), whether they are formed simultaneously or sequentially (Ouspenskaia et al., 2016) and if there is a hierarchy organising their interaction.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on stem cell niche organization.

claim: The induction of a transient, short-lived niche by HSCs in zebrafish was recently reported to occur by major morphological remodelling of perivascular endothelial cells.
source: The induction of a transient, short-lived niche by HSCs in zebrafish was recently reported to occur by major morphological remodelling of perivascular endothelial cells (Tamplin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study on HSC niche formation.
